jute.origin: Of the many species in the genus Corchorus, only two are grown commercially for fiber: Corchorus capsularis, called white jute, and Corchorus olitorius, called tossa jute. Tossa fiber is generally softer, stronger and more lustrous, while white jute is paler. Both grow best in humid tropical lowlands and river deltas. India and Bangladesh together produce roughly 90 to 95% of the world supply, with smaller production in countries such as Nepal and Myanmar. Jute is a high-volume, low-cost fiber used mainly for packaging and industrial textiles.
jute.structure: Jute is a lignocellulosic bast fiber. Typical analyses give about 58 to 63% alpha-cellulose, 21 to 24% hemicellulose and 12 to 14% lignin, with small fractions of wax, pectin, protein and mineral matter. What is traded as a jute fiber is a strand of many ultimate cells, each only a few millimeters long, cemented together by lignin and hemicellulose. Spun jute therefore behaves as a network of bonded short cells rather than as long individual fibers. Its lignin content, several times higher than the roughly 2 to 5% reported for long hemp bast fiber, makes jute stiffer and more brittle and is associated with its tendency to yellow and weaken in light.
jute.process: Mature stems are cut, bundled and retted by submerging them in ponds, ditches or slow-moving water until microbial action loosens the fiber from the stem. The fiber is stripped, washed and dried, then graded and baled. At the mill, the brittle fiber is softened by batching: an oil and water emulsion is applied and the fiber is left to condition, which lubricates it for machine processing. Softened fiber is carded on breaker and finisher cards, drawn and spun into coarse yarns, which are woven into hessian (burlap) and sacking or used for carpet backing, twine and geotextiles.
jute.performance: Jute has good tensile strength but very low extensibility, so it resists stretching yet breaks under repeated bending and abrasion and sheds loose fiber. It is hygroscopic, absorbing moisture readily, and it rots and mildews if stored damp. Lignin makes it prone to yellowing and strength loss in sunlight. Jute is combustible and chars; flame-retardant treatments for jute fabrics are an active research area. Because of its lignin and hemicellulose, it accepts basic dyes as well as cellulose dye classes, though bright, light-fast shades are harder to achieve than on cotton.
jute.identify: Burn tests are indicative only and need fire precautions; jute burns like other cellulose fibers with a paper-like smell. Under the microscope, strands show short ultimate cells with a lumen of irregular width, and lignin stains distinguish jute from low-lignin fibers such as flax, ramie and cotton. Kenaf and other jute-like bast fibers can be confused with jute, and burlap-look fabrics may be made from polypropylene or paper yarns, which a burn test or FTIR quickly separates.
jute.labeling: In the United States, jute textile products are labeled by fiber name and percentage by weight under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act (15 U.S.C. 70 et seq.) and 16 CFR Part 303. Hessian and burlap are fabric terms, not fiber names, so a burlap-look product still needs its actual fiber content stated. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 governs fiber names on textile labels. Voluntary organic certification such as GOTS can in principle apply to jute, but much jute is traded as a commodity without chain-of-custody documentation, so origin and processing claims usually depend on supplier records.
jute.past: Jute's industrial history links Bengal and Scotland. In the 1830s, Dundee spinners found that raw jute shipped from Calcutta could be softened with a whale oil and water emulsion, making it workable on machinery originally used for flax; the process gave new use to oil from the city's declining whaling trade. Dundee became known as Juteopolis, with a large share of its workforce employed in the mills. In 1855 a British entrepreneur and a Bengali partner set up the first jute mill at Rishra on the Hooghly River near Calcutta, and by around 1895 the Bengal mills had overtaken the Scottish industry, shifting the center of manufacture to the region where the crop was grown.
